content: Health systems should be structured to address the comprehensive needs of individuals rather than focusing solely on specific diseases. These systems must also respect social preferences. People-centered care necessitates that patients are provided with the education and support required to make informed decisions and actively participate in their own care. Additionally, caregivers should be enabled to function optimally within a supportive working environment. People-centered care extends beyond the scope of patientor person-centered care. It encompasses not only clinical interactions but also the health of individuals within their communities and their critical role in shaping health policies and services. Evidence-based interventions are essential to overcome barriers and leverage facilitators to improve men's uptake of voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC). This requires effective coordination among stakeholders, as many health services fail to adequately reach adult men and adolescent boys. Lessons learned from VMMC programs can inform efforts to achieve universal health coverage by 2030, as agreed upon by the United Nations and WHO Member States. Universal health coverage aims to ensure that all individuals have access to necessary health services of sufficient quality without incurring financial hardship. Changes to service delivery or the range of services offered have been identified as effective in increasing uptake. Most approaches involve multiple components, such as home-based HIV testing, education on HIV prevention and VMMC, and follow-up with supportive messages encouraging men to seek services. Short-term intensified promotional and outreach campaigns, coupled with quality improvements like enhanced privacy, have also been implemented. Health care workers, whose competencies were improved through training, offered a broader range of services. Engaging men's female partners in sexual and reproductive health education has been another strategy. Geographic information system (GIS) data has been used to identify areas with low coverage, where targeted interventions were then implemented. These studies have been conducted in diverse settings, including health care facilities, communities, homes, and schools, with a focus on adolescents. Economic compensation has been offered in some interventions, either for undergoing VMMC or for seeking counseling on VMMC at health facilities. Compensation has included fixed amounts, lottery prizes, food, transportation, or subsidized vouchers for male circumcision. Fixed compensation to cover transportation or opportunity costs was associated with higher uptake of VMMC among adult men, whereas lottery-based or variable compensation did not yield similar results. Economic compensation can help address access barriers, such as transportation costs, but singling out VMMC for compensation may not be sustainable or appropriate as countries strive for universal health coverage. Decisions regarding the use, type, and amount of compensation require community engagement, input from local stakeholders, and consideration of the specific context. A policy review on men's health and services revealed that while most national strategic plans acknowledge the importance of gender mainstreaming in HIV-related interventions, few address the need to engage men. Across HIV services, from prevention to testing and treatment, there is a significant gender gap in access. Men's limited use of health services may be influenced by prevailing gender norms, structural barriers, poor access, opportunity costs, and limited focus on men's health issues in policies. Preventing HIV through safe voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) for adolescent boys and men in generalized HIV epidemics remains a priority. The WHO health systems building blocks have been used as a framework for detailed considerations in transitioning to sustainable adolescent-focused services. Partnering with adolescents, local community organizations, and other sectors can enhance access for this demographic. In 2018, 7 million people were newly infected with HIV, with 60% residing in sub-Saharan Africa and nearly half of new infections occurring in East and Southern Africa. The urgency of ending the spread of HIV is underscored by global goals to reduce incidence, particularly in high-burden areas. The UNAIDS 2016–2021 strategy aims to end the AIDS epidemic as a public health threat by 2030. It targets 90% of people knowing their HIV status, 90% of those infected receiving antiretroviral treatment (ART), and 90% of those on treatment achieving viral suppression by 2020, with coverage increasing to 95% by 2030. Prevention goals include reducing annual new HIV infections to fewer than 500,000 globally by 2020 and fewer than 200,000 by 2030. Achieving these goals will require a combination of interventions, including condom use, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), and VMMC, as well as population-focused strategies for key populations and adolescent girls and young women. The protective effect of VMMC against heterosexual HIV acquisition in men is well-established, but evidence is less clear regarding its impact on men who have sex with men. WHO's 2016 recommendation states that VMMC is not recommended for preventing HIV transmission in sex between men due to insufficient evidence of its protective effect during receptive anal intercourse. However, men who have sex with men may still benefit from VMMC if they also engage in vaginal sex with women. Research since then has not supported a change in this recommendation. As higher levels of adult VMMC coverage are achieved, programs will shift to offering VMMC to new cohorts of adolescents. Reorienting VMMC delivery for adolescents and addressing its impact and safety will respond to ministries' requests for guidance on transitioning to sustainable adolescent services. Countries must consider this transitional phase in the context of delivering other adolescent services, aligning with broader efforts to strengthen adolescent health services in line with universal health coverage goals. Innovative methods of male circumcision have been tested and expanded since 2007 to simplify the procedure, broaden the range of authorized health care workers, and increase the choice of methods available. WHO's 2013 recommendation on prequalified devices has been supported by further evidence on the safety of surgical circumcision methods, including age-specific data. After a decade of experience and a changing context of HIV prevention, it is timely to review the 2007 VMMC recommendations. Many countries are now focusing on sustaining VMMC coverage, particularly among uncircumcised adolescent boys. Despite progress, uptake of VMMC among adult men has often lagged behind that of adolescents. Lessons learned from enhancing VMMC uptake among men may inform programming for other health interventions, including HIV testing and prevention, that have also had limited uptake among adult men.
